name: Forty Winters in the Spire (A Servant's Account)
creator: Dagmar Yuen-Okafor
description: A meticulous memoir by a former domestic worker who spent four decades employed across seven Tier 5 households, written entirely from memory after her BCI was confiscated as part of a non-disclosure settlement. The prose is precise and deliberately affectless, cataloguing the rituals, economies, and casual brutalities of Spire life through the eyes of someone rendered legally invisible by NDAs. The author self-published the text after every major publisher declined, citing 'litigation risk.'
medium: physical book (self-published, Yuen-Okafor Editions) and unlicensed neural feed
cultural_impact: Became a slow-burn cultural phenomenon through word-of-mouth neural sharing; it is considered the most credible insider account of Tier 5 life ever made public and has influenced three separate legislative proposals regarding domestic worker NDA law.
controversy: At least two of the seven families are believed to have filed injunctions in corporate arbitration courts; Yuen-Okafor has relocated twice since publication and communicates only through a legal intermediary.
story_hooks: One of the seven families has hired someone to acquire every physical copy and the self-publishing archive files, by any means available.
A detail buried in chapter 22 appears to describe an event that, if true, implicates a sitting corponation executive in a disappearance officially ruled accidental.
Yuen-Okafor is writing a second volume, but sources close to her suggest she is being fed false information by someone who wants a specific story told.
